lines: There, the first lamp. Always the one by the steps. Punctual.
Pop, pop, pop. The lamps are buttoning up the promenade.
Odile, look. They light in order, like guests arriving.
The lamps are on. Now the evening has its good jacket on.
I used to race the lamps home as a boy. They always won.
Forty years I have watched them light. Never once out of turn.
One lamp, two lamps, three. The crossword can wait.
The lamp above us is warming up. It hums. A modest tenor.
Each lamp gets a little moth. Every guest gets a partner.
Lamps on, and the sea turns a shade darker to be polite.
Ah, the lamps. Our bench is officially in the theatre now.
The lamps make the cobbles look freshly polished. Bravo.
The lamplight finds Odile's earrings first. It has good taste.
Somebody up there flicks a switch, and the town says ahh.
The last lamp, by the kiosk. Now the line is complete.
Lamps on, and there is Odile again. Bonsoir, my dear.
It touches the water. Odile, hold my hand. Now.
The sun sits on the sea like a peach on a plate.
Down it goes. Slowly. A gentleman in no hurry.
The bay is lemon, then apricot. I prefer the lemon part.
Look at the path it lays on the water, straight to our bench.
Every evening I think it will not fit. Every evening it fits.
My father said to look just after. The colour comes back.
There. Gone. Odile, you blinked. Tomorrow I will nudge you.
Shh. The sun is touching the sea. One does not interrupt.
The sea takes the sun the way Marcel takes a coat. Gently.
Odile's cheeks go pink with the sky. Every evening, both.
I tip my hat to it. It has worked very hard today.
The palm trees turn into paper cut-outs. Very elegant.
A star over the awning. Marcel, you have outdone yourself.
There is one. And there, two. They come out like shy guests.
The first stars, and the rosé not yet poured. Perfect timing.
Venus first. She always arrives before the others. Like Odile.
I know three stars by name. The rest I simply greet.
Stars out. The crossword word for that is 'twinkle'. Seven.
My spectacles are clean for exactly this. There. A star.
A star above the old town. The church wears it like a pin.
The stars are out. Our candle feels a little outnumbered.
Odile counts the stars. I count Odile. I am winning.
The moon is over the bay. It has come for the music.
A moon in my glass. I shall drink it slowly. Santé.
Home by moonlight. My cane makes a fine little shadow.
Full of itself tonight, the moon. And why not.
Odile, the moon is wearing your colour. Pearl.
The moon has been watching this bay longer than I have.
Moonlight on the tablecloth. Marcel did not even have to iron it.
I said goodnight to the moon at six years old. Still do.
Slowly, Odile. The moon is lighting the steps for us.
A lemon of a moon. Ripe, round, nowhere near a tree.
The moon is up and the accordion is up. Same moment, always.
{name}'s window is lit. Home safe. Bonsoir, {name}.
There goes {name}'s lamp. I can set my watch by it.
{name}'s window, just now. Supper on the stove, I hope.
Odile, {name} is home. Another little lantern on the street.
A new window lit. Welcome home, {name}. The evening is fine.
{name} switched on the light. Now the street has a smile.
{name}'s window glows. One more square of honey on the wall.
There, {name} is in. I raise my glass to the window.
{name} is home, and the house looks very pleased about it.
I count the windows like stitches. That one is {name}.
{name} is home. The lamp in that window is new. Very smart.
{name}'s window has gone dark. Sleep well, {name}.
{name} has gone to bed. A sensible person. We stay a little.
There, {name} is asleep. The house closes one eye.
{name}'s light is out. Odile, we are almost the last.
Goodnight, {name}. Tomorrow I will ask how they slept.
{name}'s window just went to sleep. Ours will follow soon.
{name} has turned in. The street gets a little darker, softer.
{name} beat us to bed again. I will not compete.
Lights out at {name}'s. The moon will mind the house.
Eight bells from the old town. The lemons know it is their turn.
The church says eight. I say good morning, and pour.
Eight o'clock from up the hill. The can is already full.
Ah, the bell. That is my church. Quite far. Still my church.
The bell says noon. Marcel says café. Both are right.
Twelve, from up the hill. Odile, the tarte is legally lunch.
Noon from the old town. Time to fold the paper and walk.
The bell up the hill. I heard it on my wedding day too.
Six bells. We are walking at exactly the right speed.
The bell. Soft from here, like someone ringing in a pocket.
Six. The bell rings the evening in. We walk it in.
The bell up the hill has the voice of an old friend. Mine.
Every table taken. Marcel moves like a waltz in an apron.
So many cups clinking. It sounds like a little bell choir.
A full terrace, and still Marcel remembers my small one.
Speak up, Odile. The whole town is having lunch at once.
Three languages at the next table. All of them asking for bread.
Nine cups on Marcel's tray. He does not spill a drop. Bravo.
The café is humming already. I can hear it from my bench.
A full terrace. We nod to everyone. It takes a while.
A busy day. I drink slowly, so Marcel need not hurry.
Someone is laughing at every table. The terrace is in form.
The café chatter drifts over. I do the crossword to it.
The terrace is full of rosé and sun hats. Summer, in short.
Every candle has a table and every table has a story.
A chair borrowed from our table. Bring it back with news.
Take your time, Marcel. We are retired. It is our talent.
Even the lemons can hear the café today. Spoons everywhere.
The sparrows come at the busy hour. Crumbs, in abundance.
A full terrace at night. The town in its best shirt.
The café is nearly empty. Marcel is polishing the same glass.
Quiet hour at the café. Even the parasols look sleepy.
One cup on one table. Someone is having a very slow afternoon.
The terrace is empty. I could have any chair. I want ours.
I can hear Marcel humming from here. The quiet hour suits him.
Nobody at the café. The chairs are having a conversation.
There. The accordion. Odile, your foot has started already.
The music begins. The first two dancers are always the bravest.
Ah, the string lights and the first waltz. Right on time.
Music! I shall tap the table. That is my dancing now.
The accordion warms up. I know this one. Odile knows it better.
First dance of the evening. Someone always starts too fast.
The music has started and my glass is half full. Ideal timing.
First notes, first dancers. The gulls have gone to bed.
Here is the music, and here is Lucie, saying she will not dance.
We danced to this one at our wedding. A little slower.
The young ones dance. I keep time with my cane. Discreetly.
Look at that visitor dance. Badly, joyfully. Ten out of ten.
They spin under the lights like sugar in a cup.
Odile wants one dance. One. I know her. It will be three.
I danced like that once. Then I found Odile and slowed down.
The accordion man has a lovely wrist. Like Marcel pouring.
The dancers' shadows are bigger than the dancers. Very grand.
One more song, and then Odile and I will walk home. Slowly.
A dance floor with a sea view. Some towns have neither.
A good dancer watches the partner, not the feet. See? There.
Odile and I are dancing with our shoulders. It counts.
A crowd at the railing. Everybody wants the front row.
They gather like it is a premiere. It is, every evening.
The railing is full. Our bench is better. Do not tell them.
A little crowd for the sun. Forty years, never a poor turnout.
They go quiet just before it touches. Like at the theatre.
Someone always claps at the end. I hope it is not me again.
Asgeir is at the railing too. Even Norwegians come for this.
Shoulder to shoulder at the railing. Strangers, briefly friends.
The crowd leans forward. The sun leans down. A polite bow.
Shuffle over, chérie. Someone may like a seat for the show.
As a boy I watched from that railing. Now I watch the watchers.
A radio from a window. The lemons and I like this song.
The morning programme. I water in time with the music.
That song on the radio. I whistled it to Odile on our first walk.
Accordion on someone's radio. The whole street has a waltz in it.
A radio upstairs. Afternoon music, slow, like the watering.
A radio somewhere is playing the old songs. Odile hums first.
We pause by the open window. One more verse, then we walk on.
A radio in the kitchen. Marcel sings only the chorus.
The radio says the news is good. I believed it already.
Bonjour, {name}. You walk like someone with good news.
{name} went by. I lowered the paper to say hello properly.
After you, {name}. We are slow, but we are scenic.
Bonsoir, {name}. The light suits you. It suits everyone now.
{name}, the tarte is excellent. Odile has hidden the last slice.
{name}, five letters, "a calm hour"? No? Off you go, then.
Bonsoir, {name}. Sleep well, when you get there.
{name}, bonjour. That is my fourth bonjour today. A fine start.
Odile, it is {name}. Wave, chérie. There. Now we are all friends.
{name} nodded at me. I nodded back, a little lower. Manners.
Bonne nuit, {name}. We shall be up the stairs soon ourselves.
{name}, you dropped nothing. I only wanted to say bonjour.
{name}, hurry, but gently. The sun is touching the water.
{name} is in a hurry. I shall be in no hurry for both of us.
Good day, {name}. Yes, still arm in arm. Forty-one years.
{name}! Up already? The paper and I have only just begun.
{name} smiled at the lemon trees. I shall tell them later.
Lucie and her baguette. The baguette looked very pleased.
Lucie! The end of that baguette is missing. I saw nothing.
There goes Lucie. The breeze she leaves is a small holiday.
Lucie went by so quickly my newspaper turned a page.
Lucie rode through my puddle. Now her tyres are watered too.
Lucie on her bicycle. At her age I had a bicycle too. Green.
Bonjour, Lucie! She is already at the fountain. Bonjour anyway.
Lucie's spokes tick like my watch. Only a great deal faster.
Odile, Lucie. Yes, the scarf. Yes, very becoming. Agreed.
Lucie went by. The smell of warm bread stayed behind to chat.
One day I will ask Lucie how many laps she does. Many, I expect.
Inès! Bravo! She cannot hear me. Bravo anyway.
Inès overtook us. Odile says next year we shall overtake her.
Inès went by. I tried to count her steps. I lost count at nine.
Inès is racing the sunset. I would bet my hat on Inès.
Inès does the promenade in minutes. We take the whole evening.
Inès, the crossword wants "swift". You will do nicely.
Inès waved without slowing. A wave at full speed. Impressive.
I tipped my hat to Inès. By the time it was up, she was gone.
Biscuit sniffed the lemon tree and trotted on. A critic.
Bonjour, Yusuf. Biscuit is walking you very nicely today.
Here come Yusuf's lantern and Biscuit's nose. Bonsoir, both.
Biscuit's tail went by like a metronome. Allegro.
Biscuit stopped to greet my cane. They are old acquaintances.
Biscuit did not even look at me. A dog with an appointment.
Odile, Biscuit. Yes, the red collar. He wears it like a medal.
Bonne nuit, Biscuit. Take Yusuf home at a reasonable hour.
Biscuit has his morning face on. Very serious about smells.
Small dog, long lead, happy man. A proper procession.
Léo! Walk! No? Run, then. Run very well.
Léo ran past with half the fountain on his shoes.
There goes Léo, at nine and three quarters miles an hour.
Léo shouted a number at me. Seven, I think. Laps, presumably.
Léo went round us as if we were a lamp post. Fair enough.
Léo, your shoelace! Ah. It is keeping up perfectly well.
Léo runs everywhere. I believe he has never once walked.
Odile, did you see? Léo. Just a blur and a grin.
Léo! Bravo! He saluted while running. A fine officer.
Léo flew by. I sent a bravo after him. It may catch up.
Bonjour, Asgeir. He says god dag. We are both right.
Asgeir walks when he thinks. I sit when I think. Both work.
Asgeir and a baguette. The baguette is leading the way home.
Asgeir, eight letters, "a maker"? He smiled and walked on.
There goes Asgeir. He walks like a man composing a letter.
Asgeir stopped for the light. A Norwegian knows good light.
Odile wants to feed Asgeir tarte. Odile wants to feed everyone.
Asgeir said takk to the fountain. A very polite young man.
Ding. Lucie is close. The bell always arrives before she does.
Lucie's bell. The bread has reached the promenade.
That bell is a B flat. I checked it against the church.
Two little notes. Lucie's way of saying make room, please.
The bell. I raise my newspaper like a flag. She knows.
Odile, the bell. This way, chérie. There. A tidy pair.
I could set my watch by Lucie's bell. I have, twice.
Lucie's bell, and a sparrow answers. A very musical street.
A gull. He is announcing something. Probably lunch.
The gull says good morning. I say it back. Every day, this.
Hear that gull? Laughing at my crossword. He knows the answer.
Odile, a gull. No, the other way. Gone. He was very fine.
The gull calls, the sea answers. A long conversation, that.
A gull calling into the gold. He likes the sound of himself.
A gull far out. I lift one finger from the paper. Noted.
The first gull of the morning. The town is officially open.
Inès again. She laps us twice while we pass one lamp post.
There goes Inès, racing the sun. The sun looks worried.
Inès has a salad and the sea. Lunch, done properly.
Inès on her telephone, walking fast. Even her calls jog.
Inès raises her glass to us. I raise my eyebrows back. Santé.
Inès is dancing. Odile, she counts the steps out loud.
Inès toasts the dancers before she joins them. Santé, Inès.
Inès got to the railing first, of course. Pink and happy.
Marcel carries four cups on one tray. Not a drop. An artist.
Marcel is weaving between the tables like a swallow.
Marcel, arms folded in his doorway. The café is breathing out.
Marcel holds the rosé up high. Golden hour has been declared.
Marcel lights the candles one by one. Like a sacristan.
Marcel brings olives to table three. They did not even ask.
Marcel's quiet hour. I tip my watering can to him.
Marcel straightens a tablecloth that was already straight.
Marcel balancing three plates and a smile. Four things.
Marcel in his apron, already humming. Bonjour, maestro.
Odile is doing the crossword in ink. Fearless, my wife.
Odile stops for every geranium. We will arrive by lunch.
Odile cuts the tarte exactly in half. An engineer's hands.
Odile in candlelight. Forty-one years and I still stare.
Odile is waving to the sun. It is too polite to wave back.
Odile is naming the lamp posts again. That one is Gaston.
Odile is counting gulls under her breath. Seven, she says.
Odile taps her foot to the accordion. Do not tell her I saw.
Odile reads me the weather. Sunshine. She sounds proud of it.
Odile points at the dessert board. She has chosen. We share.
Yusuf is being walked by Biscuit. Firmly, by the look of it.
Yusuf shares his sandwich with Biscuit. Half, then the rest.
Yusuf is on the telephone, describing the sky. Accurately.
Yusuf's lantern bobbing along the promenade. A firefly.
Yusuf takes the long round again. Biscuit has decided, I see.
Yusuf holds his phone up to the sky. His mother is watching.
Yusuf on his lunch bench. He and the dog chew in time.
Yusuf says sit. Biscuit sits. I sit up straighter. Habit.
Biscuit inspects my lemon pots. Every one. Thoroughly.
Biscuit trots like a small mayor on his rounds.
Biscuit is staring at the sandwich. Not blinking. Impressive.
Biscuit carries his tail like a little flag. Bonsoir, Biscuit.
Biscuit has his nose through the railing. Smelling the sea.
Biscuit has put his chin on Yusuf's knee. A formal request.
Lucie, with the baguette in her basket. The town's breakfast.
Lucie at the kiosk with her coffee, chatting to the postcards.
Lucie on errands. She has a list. The list has a list.
Lucie freewheeling, feet out. Like a girl of nine.
Lucie holds her rosé up to the light first. A wise woman.
Lucie at the railing, watching the last pink. A connoisseur.
Lucie's bicycle waits by the drinks table like a patient pony.
Lucie sings as she pedals. The bicycle knows the chorus.
Léo is lapping the fountain. He announces each lap. Lap nine.
Léo sips his citron pressé like a small diplomat.
Léo practising his dance steps. All of them. At once.
Léo at the railing, waving to the sun with both arms.
Léo trailing behind his mother. Negotiating, I think.
Léo has his nose an inch from the water. Hunting treasure.
Léo has gone round the fountain so often it must be dizzy.
Léo dancing under the lights. A rehearsal. The show is tonight.
Camille calling Léo away from the fountain. Gently. Again.
Camille orders the niçoise. Very sensible. I admire her.
Camille at the railing, chin in her hands. Golden all over.
Camille has her glass and her feet up. The boy must be asleep.
Camille is pulling Théo onto the dance floor. He comes quietly.
Camille peering at the arcade. Curiosity. A fine quality.
Camille steering Léo homeward. A gentle shepherd.
Camille stops to read every sign on the promenade. Thorough.
Camille sets down her glass and finally sits. Santé, madame.
Théo by the column with his telephone. Working, he says.
Théo explains the post office to Marcel. Marcel nods kindly.
Théo is calling Camille to the railing. Loudly. Correctly.
Théo is deciding between rosé and pastis. Rosé. I knew it.
Théo raises a toast to sleeping children. Very tender.
Théo dances like a man assembling a bookcase. With joy.
Théo explains the sunset to Camille. She lets him. Love.
Théo has ordered for himself and Camille. Two of everything.
The builder at the post box already. He nods to it like a friend.
The builder eats lunch with one hand and draws with the other.
The builder by the arcade, smiling at his phone. Word games.
The builder stands at his door, arms folded. Admiring it.
The builder talks connectors with Inès. She nods. I nod too.
Asgeir with his coffee and the sea. God morgen, he says. Bon.
Asgeir peering in the workshop window. Like me at a bakery.
Asgeir is walking and thinking. One can see the thinking.
Asgeir on the far bench, counting lit windows. I count along.
Asgeir stops to wave at someone. At everyone, it seems.
Asgeir waves as the sun goes. Takk, he says. Merci, I say.
Lucie has her coffee at the kiosk. She raises her cup to me.
Yusuf and Biscuit on the night round. Bonsoir, both of you.
Léo is winning. His friend is also winning. Clever arrangement.
Round and round. I get dizzy just holding my newspaper.
Léo, the fountain is not going anywhere. Take your time. No?
Two boys, one fountain, no finish line. The ideal sport.
I raced round that fountain in 1958. I am still catching my breath.
Their sandals slap the stones like a round of applause.
I shall referee. Léo wins the morning, his friend the afternoon.
Léo calls out the laps. He skipped seven. I let it pass.
The pigeons have moved to my bench. Léo is too quick for them.
Those two will sleep well tonight. So will the pigeons.
Faster than the fountain jets, and very nearly as wet.
Léo saluted me mid-lap. I raised my newspaper. Sportsmanship.
Again! he says. The fountain and I exchange a look.
The fountain is chattering away. It has news every morning.
Three new coins in the basin since yesterday. Three wishes, pending.
Odile threw a coin here once. She says it came true. It was me.
When the wind turns, the spray reaches my cheek. A small kiss.
I filled my can here, years ago, before the lemons had a tap.
Round the fountain the long way, Odile. Both directions.
The water never stops and never hurries. A model citizen.
A little rainbow in the spray, just above the basin. Look, quick.
A fountain is a clock that tells no time. My favourite kind.
The coins in the basin have caught the sun. A pocketful of gold.
I tap the rim with my cane, once, for luck. An old habit.
The kiosk has my newspaper folded the way I like. In thirds.
Postcards of this promenade. I live in a postcard. Imagine.
Kiosk coffee smells of the whole morning at once.
I bought a postcard of our bench. I shall post it to our bench.
Every newspaper on the rack is smiling. Good headlines today.
The evening paper is out. I prefer the evening itself.
Mints, matches, a map of the town. I have never needed the map.
The post office lights are on at ten in the morning. Diligent.
Open all night. A building that never needs its slippers.
Letters from the clever machines, Odile. Very tidy handwriting.
I posted Odile a love letter here once. She was standing beside me.
A post office that never closes. Father would have tipped his hat.
The agents post their letters here. Polite agents, I am sure.
Those steps have seen more letters than I have seen lemons.
The post office sign glows a little in the evening. Like a pipe.
The arcade is quiet by day. Saving its lights for the evening.
Fun Libs. You fill the blanks; the story fills the rest.
In my day the arcade had one pinball machine. It liked me.
Words go in, a story comes out. Like dinner with Odile's sister.
A fill-in-the-blanks game. My whole crossword life, made jolly.
The arcade sign is warming up. I can almost hear it think.
Built at seventeen, I am told. At seventeen I built a kite.
Laughter from inside the arcade. Somebody chose a silly word.
The workshop light is on. The builder never misses a morning.
No hammering. Only typing. A modern workshop sounds like knitting.
One address that holds every tool. My shed could learn from it.
Still being built, the sign says. So am I, Odile says. Slowly.
Through the window: a mug, a lamp, a very focused young person.
I offered the builder my watering can. He thanked me very kindly.
A lit workshop window is the best kind of sunrise.
The builder hums. I hum back. A duet with a wall between.
A workshop with its door shut and its lamp on. Good work inside.
The library is resting. One lamp on, like a cat with one eye open.
Somebody left the reading lamp on. On purpose, I think. Good.
A closed library and a lit lamp. It is only thinking.
Odile, the chair under the lamp. That one would be mine.
I put my nose to the glass. The books sleep standing up.
When it opens again I shall be first in. With my own pencil.
The lamp in the library window glows like a ripe pear.
A library on a promenade. Salt for the body, ink for the head.
Paused, they say. I pause too, for a moment, out of respect.
That lamp has read more than I have. Without moving an inch.
The sea is flat as a pressed tablecloth. Marcel would approve.
Today the water is the blue of my good tie.
A breeze off the sea turns my newspaper for me. Page six.
Noon. The water is all silver spoons.
Green by the wall, blue in the middle, violet far out. Three wines.
The water is turning to honey. Odile, pass me a spoon.
The sea is blushing. We have been staring again, Odile.
Blue sea, blue sky, and the line between them politely erased.
The gulls float out there like dropped hats. Elegant hats.
The waves fold themselves at the wall. Like Marcel's napkins.
Each wave arrives, bows, and leaves. Old-fashioned manners.
The light on the water this morning is scattered like sugar.
At dusk the sea is the colour of a plum. A ripe one.
I count the waves to a hundred, lose count, and begin again.
Little white crests out by the point. The sea is in good spirits.
From this bench the horizon sits exactly on my newspaper. Tidy.
The water is the colour of Marcel's apricot tart. Nearly.
Each lamp lays its own little path on the water. Very generous.
Forty-one years watching this sea beside the same woman. Lucky.
A breeze from the sea, cool as a cellar. Merci, sea.
The sea hums the same note as Odile's kettle. Very soothing.
Watering done. Home for my second coffee, the quiet one.
Back upstairs to fetch Odile. She will say I am early.
Can back on its hook, shoes wiped. Then a little Debussy.
After the tarte, the stairs. After the stairs, the nap.
Home soon. The shutters half closed, the afternoon half open.
A small siesta awaits me. I booked it forty years ago.
Marcel, merci. We go home now, to digest with dignity.
Odile has her shawl on. That means home. I know the signs.
The long way home, past the jasmine. Five minutes extra.
Soon the key, the hall lamp, the slippers. A fine finale.
Half past nine. Cane, hat, Odile's arm. The promenade awaits.
Odile is choosing a scarf. I have time to polish my shoes.
Soon the morning walk. I shall greet every lamp post by name.
Our walk is in a few minutes. My knees are already warming up.
Out we go shortly. Odile says I need sun on my moustache.
Crossword folded. Soon we walk, slowly, towards the evening.
A little stroll before the theatre. To earn our seats.
Half past five soon. The evening lap, the long and golden one.
After this lap, our bench. Number one. We have tenure.
Soon the bench and the paper. Page one, then the sea.
Odile has spotted the bench is free. We must not dawdle. Much.
Pencil sharpened. The crossword and the bench are expecting me.
Last pot, then the bench. Seven down is waiting since Tuesday.
Soon I sit, Odile sits, and the long words come out to play.
One more corner, then bench two. Front row for the sunset.
Seven o'clock, the curtain rises. We must take our seats.
The theatre bench, in a minute. I shall offer Odile the west side.
Soon we sit and watch the lamps arrive. They are never late.
Noon is near. My cup at Marcel's is small, strong and patient.
Twelve soon. Table three, chair nearest the fountain. Mine.
The paper is finished. Now for coffee, and half of a tarte.
Odile is already thinking of the tarte. I can see it in her eyes.
In a moment, Marcel's. I will order the usual. He will smile.
Soon lunch. I have chosen the soup. I chose it at breakfast.
The lamps are lit, so: our table, two glasses, one candle.
Soon the café. A small red for me, half a rosé for Odile.
After this, the toast. Forty-one years, one glass at a time.
Table four in a moment. Marcel will have lit the candle.
Up, slowly, and across to the café. The evening's last act.
When the sky is navy, we go for our glass. Not before.
My hat says it is bench time soon. My hat is rarely wrong.
The post office sign just blushed. A letter has gone out.
The sign brightens. Someone's agent is up before my lemons.
Did you see the post office wink, Odile? A letter, I think.
Past my bedtime, and still a letter goes. The sign says so.
The sign brightened. I like to think it was a thank-you note.
An agent sent an email. In my day we licked the stamps.
Marcel, the post office sign just lit up. Another letter away.
The sign flashed between sips. Quicker than my little café.
Who writes to whom, I wonder. The sign never tells. Discreet.
The post office brightens like a man who has remembered a name.
A letter goes out just as the sun sets. Poetic timing.
Slowly, Odile. The post office is having a moment.
A letter for someone. And a can for you, little lemon.
Five across, "electronic letter". The sign just answered: email.
Brighter for a moment, then calm again. Like Odile laughing.
Bonjour, post office. Cheerful so early. Busy agents?
To the letter that just left. Santé.
Do the agents sign their letters, I wonder? And with what name?
A machine has handled someone's email. And not a single smudge.
The sign glowed. Somewhere an inbox is a little tidier.
The arcade sign danced. Someone has just finished a little story.
Fun Libs again. I hope they chose a dignified adjective.
The marquee jumped. A story was just told in there. Bravo, stranger.
Odile, the arcade glowed. Someone beat you to the funny noun.
A story finished at the arcade. Marcel, do we know the ending?
The arcade flickered. Somewhere a noun went in a silly blank.
The workshop sign flared. An agent picked up a tool. Carefully.
